opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, part of it is just habit. I started out in computer graphics and physics-based animation, then moved into robotics, and for most of my career the field was simply called robotics. "Embodied AI" became a popular term much more recently, and to me it sometimes feels like a new label on something people have been working on for decades.

But there's a more substantive reason too. When people say "embodied AI," the emphasis tends to fall on the AI part: the models, the data, the scaling. Those things matter a lot, and much of my own work is about bringing learning, and now large foundation models, into robots. Still, a robot is not just a model with a body attached. It's a physical system. You have motors that overheat, gears with backlash, sensors that are noisy, contacts that are hard to simulate, batteries, safety constraints. If you ignore all of that and only think about intelligence in the abstract, the system won't work in the real world.

So when I say "robotics," I'm reminding myself and others that this is a full-stack problem. Hardware, control, perception, learning, and the AI brain all have to come together. The intelligence has to be grounded in the physics and the engineering. In that sense, robotics is the bigger and more honest word for what we're trying to do: build machines that can actually act usefully and safely in the physical world. Embodied AI is an important part of that, but I'd call it a part rather than the whole.

r001.rationale: The response says physical contacts are hard to simulate, but does not state that embodied AI can include robots that exist only in simulation.

r002.rationale: It ties the preference for “robotics” to the physical engineering and real-world operation of robots, describing robotics as the full-stack work of building machines that act in the physical world.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's mostly a matter of habit and of where I come from. I did my PhD in robotics, I've worked in robotics my whole career, and the word just feels more concrete to me. When I say "robot," everyone knows what I mean: a physical machine that has to move, grasp, balance, deal with gravity and friction and all the messiness of the real world.

"Embodied AI" is a newer term, and I understand why people like it. It emphasizes that the intelligence is the point and the body is the vehicle for that intelligence. And I actually agree with that framing in spirit. The big change in the last few years is that robotics is no longer just about control and mechanics. It's about learning, about foundation models, about data. So in that sense embodied AI captures something real.

But I'm a little cautious about the term for two reasons. First, it can make the problem sound more solved than it is. When you say "AI," people immediately think of ChatGPT, and they imagine we're one step away from a robot that does everything. The reality is that the physical world is unforgiving. A language model that makes a small mistake produces a slightly wrong sentence. A robot that makes a small mistake drops the cup, or falls down the stairs. The body is not a detail you add at the end. It's the hard part.

Second, "robotics" reminds me that this is an engineering discipline with a long history. People in control theory, in mechanical design, in perception, solved many hard problems before deep learning arrived, and a lot of that knowledge still matters. I don't want to throw that away just because we have a new name.

So I'd say I'm not opposed to "embodied AI." If someone uses it, I know exactly what they're talking about, and we're probably working on the same thing. I just prefer "robotics" because it keeps me honest about the physical world, and because, frankly, that's what I've always called it.

r002.rationale: It says robotics keeps attention on the physical world, but does not attribute Jie Tan’s preference to his work extending beyond simulation into the physical world.

astra-6.text:
I prefer “robotics” because it makes the problem concrete. We’re trying to build machines that can perceive the physical world, make decisions, and act in it. Intelligence is a big part of that, but so are control, hardware, and reliability. A robot has to deal with all of those together.

“Embodied AI” emphasizes the intelligence side, and it’s a useful perspective. But for me, the goal is to get a robot to do something useful in the real world. Robotics is simply the more direct name for that.

r002.rationale: It explains that Tan prefers “robotics” because his goal is to build machines that act in the physical world and do useful work in the real world.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to call it robotics because that makes the goal concrete: we want to build robots that can do useful things in the physical world. AI is a very important part of that, but it’s only part of the challenge. You also have hardware, control, sensing, and the problem of making everything work together reliably.

Embodied AI is a useful term, especially when we’re talking about intelligence that learns through interaction with the world. There’s a lot of overlap. But for me, robotics keeps the focus on the whole system and what it can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response describes embodied AI as intelligence learning through interaction with the world, but does not say it can include robots that exist only in simulation.

r002.rationale: The response ties the preference for “robotics” to building useful robots in the physical world and addressing hardware, control, sensing, and system reliability.
